folder: Principles of Diagnostic Medicine I Exam 4

items.section_title: 17.4 · Objective a — Normal structures on computed tomography and the angiogram
items.html: Why the trachea and bronchi are dark on computed tomography. Air and gas are low attenuation, so the air-filled trachea and bronchi show dark on computed tomography.

src.question: A 44-year-old's lung-window computed tomography shows the trachea and main bronchi as dark circles. Why are they dark?
src.explanation: Air and gas are low attenuation, so the air-filled trachea and bronchi show dark on computed tomography.

items.section_title: 20.2 · Objective a — The four lung volumes and the four lung capacities
items.html: Total lung capacity is the sum of all four volumes. Total lung capacity, the maximum volume the lungs can hold, is the sum of all four volumes: tidal, inspiratory reserve, expiratory reserve and residual.
cites: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 13 and 23

src.question: A 60-year-old woman's report lists the maximum volume of air her lungs can hold. Which volumes add up to it?
src.key: All four volumes, residual volume included
src.explanation: Correct. Total lung capacity, the maximum volume the lungs can hold, is the sum of all four volumes: tidal, inspiratory reserve, expiratory reserve and residual.

items.section_title: 20.6 · Objective d — Interpreting a report: the stepwise read and three cases
items.html: A low total lung capacity is restriction. A low total lung capacity is restriction; with a normal ratio there is no obstruction alongside it.
cites: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 43 and 32

src.question: A 57-year-old woman's total lung capacity is 62% of predicted (normal 80% to 120%), with an FEV1/FVC (forced expiratory volume in one second over forced vital capacity) ratio of 88% (normal above 80%). What is the basic interpretation?
src.explanation: Correct. A low total lung capacity is restriction, and her ratio is normal, so there is no obstruction alongside it.

items.section_title: 20.3 · Objective a — Spirometry: how it is done and the forced values
items.html: The spirometry breath out. After a maximal breath in, the patient exhales forcefully, as fast as possible, and keeps going for at least 6 seconds.
cites: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 24, 29 and 21

src.question: A 45-year-old man is coached through spirometry. After he breathes in as deeply as he can, what is he asked to do?
src.key: Blow out as hard and fast as he can for 6 seconds or more
src.explanation: Correct. After a maximal breath in, the patient exhales forcefully, as fast as possible, and keeps going for at least 6 seconds.

items.section_title: 20.7 · Objective e — The role of pulmonary function testing in diagnosis and monitoring
items.html: Lung volumes diagnose restriction. Lung volumes are the standard test responsible for diagnosing restrictive lung disease; spirometry diagnoses obstruction and the diffusing capacity pulmonary vascular disease.
cites: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 18 and 43

src.question: A 63-year-old man's spirometry suggests restriction. Which standard test is responsible for diagnosing restrictive lung disease?
src.explanation: Correct. Lung volumes are the standard test responsible for diagnosing restrictive lung disease; spirometry diagnoses obstruction and the diffusing capacity pulmonary vascular disease.

items.section_title: 19.2 · Objective a — The oxygen-hemoglobin curve and base excess
items.html: Why base excess is reported. Base excess or deficit, the sum of the buffer anions in whole blood, is critically important in determining respiratory against nonrespiratory changes in acid-base balance.
cites: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 40, 10 and 42

src.question: A 58-year-old's arterial blood gas includes the base excess or deficit. Why is that value reported?
src.key: To tell respiratory from nonrespiratory change
src.explanation: Correct. Base excess or deficit, the sum of the buffer anions in whole blood, is critically important in determining respiratory against nonrespiratory changes in acid-base balance.

items.section_title: 19.7 · Objective f — Calculating the anion gap
items.html: An anion gap with the potassium given. Anion gap = sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate) = 136 minus (99 plus 19) = 136 minus 118 = 18; the potassium is not in the formula.
cites: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 46

src.question: A 67-year-old has serum sodium 136 mEq/L (normal 135 to 148 mEq/L), potassium 4.5 mEq/L (normal 3.6 to 5.2 mEq/L), chloride 99 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L) and bicarbonate 19 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What is his anion gap?
src.explanation: Correct. Anion gap = sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate) = 136 minus (99 plus 19) = 136 minus 118 = 18; the potassium is not in the formula.

items.section_title: 19.7 · Objective f — Calculating the anion gap
items.html: Two anion gaps worked. Anion gap = sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate) = 140 minus (104 plus 24) = 140 minus 128 = 12, inside the normal 9 to 15. Anion gap = sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate) = 138 minus (112 plus 16) = 138 minus 128 = 10, inside the normal 9 to 15; the potassium is not in the formula.
cites: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 46

src.question: A 49-year-old's serum sodium is 140 mEq/L (normal 135 to 148 mEq/L), chloride 104 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L) and bicarbonate 24 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What is his anion gap?
src.explanation: Correct. Anion gap = sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate) = 140 minus (104 plus 24) = 140 minus 128 = 12, inside the normal 9 to 15.

also.question: A 34-year-old with several days of diarrhea has serum sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 148 mEq/L), potassium 3.4 mEq/L (normal 3.6 to 5.2 mEq/L), chloride 112 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L) and bicarbonate 16 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What is his anion gap?
also.explanation: Correct. Anion gap = sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate) = 138 minus (112 plus 16) = 138 minus 128 = 10, inside the normal 9 to 15; the potassium is not in the formula.

items.section_title: 19.6 · Objective e — Expected findings in the four disorders
items.html: Potassium in acidosis and in alkalosis. pH changes cause changes in serum potassium: in acidosis, potassium shifts into the extracellular space, causing hyperkalemia. In alkalosis potassium shifts into the intracellular space, causing hypokalemia.
cites: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 44
Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 44 and 34

src.question: A 60-year-old in severe acidosis has a serum potassium of 5.9 mEq/L (normal 3.6 to 5.2 mEq/L). What best explains the potassium?
src.key: Potassium shifting out of cells into the blood
src.explanation: Correct. pH changes cause changes in serum potassium: in acidosis, potassium shifts into the extracellular space, causing hyperkalemia.

also.question: A 50-year-old with metabolic alkalosis from vomiting has a serum potassium of 3.1 mEq/L (normal 3.6 to 5.2 mEq/L). How does the alkalosis itself move potassium?
also.key: Into the cells, lowering the serum level
also.explanation: Correct. In alkalosis potassium shifts into the intracellular space, causing hypokalemia.

items.section_title: 19.5 · Objective d — Interpreting the blood gas: pH, the steps, what moves each value, compensation
items.html: The first step. The step-wise approach to any acid-base problem starts with the pH: low is acidosis, high is alkalosis. Then: which values are outside the normal range, and do the labs fit the patient?
cites: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 49 and 21

src.question: A 59-year-old's arterial blood gas has just arrived. Taking a step-wise approach, which value is looked at first?
src.explanation: Correct. The step-wise approach to any acid-base problem starts with the pH: low is acidosis, high is alkalosis. Then: which values are outside the normal range, and do the labs fit the patient?

items.section_title: 19.8 · Objective g — The clinical significance of an abnormal anion gap
items.html: A low gap with a low albumin. A decreased anion gap can be associated with hypoalbuminemia; the gap must be corrected if albumin is abnormal, adding 2.5 mmol/L for each 1 g/dL of albumin below 4.5 g/dL.
cites: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 48, 45 and 46

src.question: A 58-year-old with cirrhosis has a low anion gap and a serum albumin of 2.5 g/dL (normal 4.5 g/dL). What must be done before the gap is interpreted?
src.key: Correct it upward for the low albumin
src.explanation: Correct. A decreased anion gap can be associated with hypoalbuminemia; the gap must be corrected if albumin is abnormal, adding 2.5 mmol/L for each 1 g/dL of albumin below 4.5 g/dL.

items.section_title: 19.4 · Objective c — Indications: when to order an arterial blood gas
items.html: How sick, from the numbers alone? The blood gas does NOT indicate the degree of any abnormality; a physical assessment is needed (treat the patient and not the labs).
cites: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 5 and 49

src.question: A 74-year-old's arterial blood gas comes back abnormal, and a student asks how sick he is from the numbers alone. What is the best reply?
src.key: The gas cannot show the degree; examine him
src.explanation: Correct. The blood gas does NOT indicate the degree of any abnormality; a physical assessment is needed (treat the patient and not the labs).

items.section_title: 19.5 · Objective d — Interpreting the blood gas: pH, the steps, what moves each value, compensation
items.html: Compensating a respiratory alkalosis. Respiratory disorders are compensated by the kidney adjusting bicarbonate reabsorption over days: respiratory alkalosis compensation is a decrease in bicarbonate.
cites: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 50 and 51

src.question: A 31-year-old woman has had a respiratory alkalosis for several days. Which compensation is expected?
src.explanation: Correct. Respiratory disorders are compensated by the kidney adjusting bicarbonate reabsorption over days: respiratory alkalosis compensation is a decrease in bicarbonate.

items.section_title: 19.3 · Objective b — Arterial against venous: why arterial, the sample and the venous values
items.html: Why a venous sample can mislead. Venous blood gives information localized to the phlebotomy site and can be affected by temperature, perfusion, movement and local infection; arterial blood is a better mixture.
cites: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 5 and 11

src.question: A 62-year-old's venous sample was drawn from an arm with an infection at the puncture site. Why might it mislead about her overall gases?
src.key: Venous blood reflects local conditions at its site
src.explanation: Correct. Venous blood gives information localized to the phlebotomy site and can be affected by temperature, perfusion, movement and local infection; arterial blood is a better mixture.
